name: Fastow (Enron): halfway, after the Board representation
description: The Enron/Fastow example with the first 8 exchanges done: the opening warning, background, LJM1, and Fastow committing to what he told the Board on June 28, 1999. Resume at question 11 of examples/enron-fastow/README.md (the Rhythms unwind), then confront him with Southampton Place.
expert_role: Executive Vice President and CFO, Enron Corp.
resume_hint: Next: question 11 in examples/enron-fastow/README.md ("How was the Rhythms hedge unwound in early 2000?"), then Part D and the Southampton Place confrontation in Part E.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Good morning. Andy Fastow. I'll be honest, nobody's told me much about what this is. Who are you with?

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Good morning, Mr. Fastow. I'm outside counsel retained by the Special Investigative Committee of Enron's Board. I represent the Committee and the company, not you personally. This conversation is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, and the company may decide to waive it and share what you tell me with others, including the government. Please keep the contents of this interview confidential. Enron does not tolerate retaliation against anyone for cooperating. Do you have any questions before we begin?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I appreciate you being clear about who you represent. I may want my own lawyer to look at some of this down the road, but I'm here and I'm happy to walk you through things. Go ahead.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: To start, could you describe your role as CFO and what the Global Finance group was responsible for?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: As CFO I was responsible for raising capital and managing the balance sheet. Global Finance did the structured transactions: finding partners and investors for our assets, hedging, keeping the company's capital working. Enron was growing fast, and my group's job was to make sure the financing kept up.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What was Michael Kopper's role in your group?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Michael was one of the managing directors in Global Finance and reported to me. He was very capable on the structured side, and he worked on a number of the partnership transactions.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Walk me through how the idea for LJM1 came about in 1999.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: We had a large gain in Rhythms NetConnections stock that we couldn't sell, and Jeff wanted it protected. Nobody in the market would hedge a position like that. So we designed a vehicle, LJM, with outside equity, that could use value already sitting in some Enron stock forward contracts to hedge the Rhythms position. It was a creative solution to a real problem.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Why did you need to be the general partner, as opposed to someone outside Enron?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: It wasn't something I was looking for. The investors needed someone who understood Enron's assets and could move quickly, and frankly, having me involved is what made the outside money comfortable. Ken and Jeff understood that, and it went through the proper channels.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Tell me about the June 28, 1999 Board meeting. What did you present?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I presented Project LJM: the partnership with outside equity, how it would hedge Rhythms, and what Enron would get in value. The Board also had to approve a waiver under the Code of Conduct because of my role. They discussed it and approved it.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What did you tell the Board about how you personally would be compensated by LJM?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: That I would commit a million dollars of my own money as general partner, and that I would not receive any current or future value from the Enron stock in the partnership. The economics of the Enron shares went to the limited partners.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: So your understanding at the time was that you would not benefit from the value of Enron stock held by LJM. Is that right?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: That's right. That was the structure, and that's what I told them.
